blocks.h: 1. The Convention and where it applies

blocks.p: The instrument is the Nairobi International Convention on the Removal of Wrecks, 2007, adopted on 18 May 2007 and in force since 14 April 2015. It operates in the Convention area - the exclusive economic zone of a State Party, or an equivalent zone not extending beyond 200 nautical miles (Article 1(1)). A State Party may extend it to its own territorial sea by declaration under Article 3(2). Domestically at the date of this examination the governing Indian statute is the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
Article 1(4) defines a wreck as something arising following upon a maritime casualty. Four categories are identified:

ul: a sunken or stranded ship;
any part of a sunken or stranded ship, including any object that is or has been on board;
any object lost at sea from a ship that is stranded, sunken or adrift at sea;
a ship that is about, or may reasonably be expected, to sink or to strand, where effective measures to assist the ship or property in danger are not already being taken.

blocks.p: Two points are commonly lost. First, the phrase "following upon a maritime casualty" is part of the definition, not scene-setting: a ship deliberately abandoned, or an object thrown overboard in the ordinary course, is not a wreck under this Convention. Second, the fourth category is anticipatory - a ship that has not yet sunk is already a wreck for these purposes if she may reasonably be expected to sink or strand and effective assistance is not already under way. That is what allows a coastal State to act before the casualty completes itself, which is usually the only cheap moment to act at all.

blocks.h: 3. Hazard - the switch that turns the Convention on

blocks.p: A wreck engages the removal machinery only if it is a hazard - Article 1(5): a condition or threat that poses a danger or impediment to navigation, or that may reasonably be expected to result in major harmful consequences to the marine environment or damage to coastal and related interests. Article 6 gives the criteria the affected State applies:

ul: the size, type and construction of the wreck, and the depth of water over it;
proximity to shipping routes, port approaches and anchorages, and the density and frequency of traffic;
the type and quantity of cargo, and the quantity and type of oil - bunkers included - on board;
the tidal range, currents and prevailing weather, and the vulnerability of port facilities;
the proximity of offshore installations, pipelines and telecommunication cables, and of areas of particular environmental sensitivity;
whether the wreck is likely to shift or deteriorate materially, and any damage already suffered.

blocks.p: The determination is therefore a reasoned assessment, not a reflex. A wreck lying deep, clear of routes, with negligible bunkers and stable structure may properly be left in place - and the Convention imposes no removal duty on its owner at all.

The Convention was written to close a gap. UNCLOS gave coastal States rights in the exclusive economic zone but no removal machinery, so a hazardous wreck beyond the territorial sea could sit there with nobody clearly obliged to move it and no guarantee that anyone solvent would pay. States were left choosing between an unfunded removal and a permanent danger. The objectives are therefore:

ul: a uniform international rule for the prompt, effective and proportionate removal of hazardous wrecks beyond the territorial sea;
cost recovery from the owner and the owner's insurer rather than from the coastal State's public funds - the polluter-pays principle applied to obstruction as well as to pollution;
legal certainty: owners and insurers know the extent of the exposure, States know the powers they hold, and both know the time limits;
financial security that is real - compulsory insurance with a right of direct action, so the remedy does not evaporate with a single-ship company.

blocks.p: The operative provisions then run as a sequence, and it is worth learning them in that order because it is the order in which a real casualty unfolds:

rows: Report the wreck - position, type, size, nature of cargo and oil on board
Master and operator, to the affected State
Determine whether the wreck is a hazard, on the listed criteria
Affected State
Locate - warn mariners, issue notices, and use all practicable means to establish the precise position
Affected State
Mark, in accordance with the internationally accepted system of buoyage, and promulgate the particulars
Affected State
Remove within a reasonable deadline set by the State; the State may intervene if the owner fails, or immediately where the hazard is severe
Registered owner, then the State

blocks.p: Behind that sequence stand the financial provisions - strict liability (Art 10), compulsory insurance with direct action (Art 12) and the time bar (Art 13). Article 9 also preserves the owner's right to contract with any salvor or contractor of his choice, subject to the State's conditions, which keeps commercial salvage inside the regime rather than displacing it.

blocks.h: 5. The shipowner - strict liability and its limits

blocks.p: Article 10 makes the registered owner strictly liable for the costs of locating, marking and removing the wreck. Fault need not be shown. The exceptions are narrow: act of war or an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon; damage wholly caused by a third party acting with intent; or wholly caused by the negligence of an authority responsible for navigational aids. Article 11 stands the Convention down where CLC 1992, the HNS, Bunkers or nuclear regimes govern the same damage.

Liability is backed by Article 12: ships of 300 GT and above must maintain insurance or other financial security, carry a certificate to that effect, and the claim may be brought directly against the insurer. The security must be at least equal to the limits of liability under the applicable limitation regime, and an insurer sued directly may invoke the defences the owner could have invoked - but not the owner's insolvency or winding up. The practical consequence is that the coastal State need not find the owner, prove negligence, or hope a single-ship company still exists: it establishes the hazard, sets the deadline and, failing compliance, removes and claims against a certified insurer whose identity it already holds. Article 10(2) preserves the owner's right to limit liability under the applicable limitation regime, and Article 13 bars claims brought more than three years after the hazard was determined, and in no case later than six years after the casualty.

blocks.h: 6. The coastal State - judgement, notice and intervention

blocks.p: The affected State decides whether the wreck is a hazard on the Article 6 criteria; informs the flag State and the registered owner; warns mariners; sets a reasonable deadline for removal and may attach conditions; and, if the owner fails to act - or immediately, where the hazard is severe - may remove the wreck itself and recover the cost. Those powers are not unlimited: measures must be proportionate to the hazard and exercised consistently with international law, and the State may not interfere with the rights of other States beyond what removal requires. Where the wreck lies in the territorial sea of a State that has not opted in under Article 3(2), the Convention does not govern and the State acts under its own domestic law - in India, the wreck and salvage provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, administered through the Receiver of Wreck.

The division is therefore clean and should be written that way: the State supplies the judgement and the compulsion; the owner supplies the work and the money. The State does not become the remover of first resort, and the owner does not decide whether the wreck is dangerous.

blocks.h: 7. Environmental implications, and what the regime does not reach

blocks.p: A wreck is a continuing environmental source rather than a single event, and that is what distinguishes it from a spill:

ul: Progressive release. Bunkers, lubricating and hydraulic oils and cargo escape as tanks corrode, sometimes years after the casualty and long after the response has stood down.
Cargo hazards. Chemicals, packaged dangerous goods and containers that break free and drift, each becoming an object within category three of the definition.
Structural contaminants. Antifouling coatings, refrigerants, batteries and other hazardous materials built into the ship.
Physical damage. Smothering and scouring of the seabed, reefs and fishing grounds; obstruction of ports, approaches and fairways; risk to fishing gear and to cables and pipelines.
Navigational risk feeding back into environmental risk. An unmarked wreck causes the next casualty, which is why marking under Article 8 sits inside an environmental instrument at all.

blocks.p: The Convention's contribution to all of this is essentially financial and procedural: strict liability plus compulsory insurance is what converts an environmental risk into a funded removal, promptly and without first litigating fault. It changes who pays and how quickly, rather than changing the physics of the casualty.

Its reach is bounded. It applies only to wrecks that are hazards, only within the Convention area unless a State has opted in for its territorial sea, and the owner's liability remains subject to the applicable limitation regime - so an exceptionally costly removal can still exceed the available fund and leave a residue for the coastal State to carry.

The limbs carry 5, 5 and 6 marks and the six-mark limb names two actors. Splitting sections 5 and 6 by actor is therefore not a stylistic choice - it is what makes both halves of the largest limb visible to the examiner. Sections 1 to 3 build the definition in the order the Convention itself uses: instrument, then definition, then trigger. Answering "define wreck" without "hazard" produces a technically correct definition that explains nothing about how the Convention works.

blocks.h: The two-part definition, and why it is two parts

blocks.p: Article 1(4) tells you what a wreck is. Article 1(5) tells you when anyone has to do anything about it. Most of the Convention - reporting, locating, marking, removal, liability - hangs off the hazard determination in Article 6, not off the definition. A wreck in deep water clear of routes, with no cargo of consequence, may be left where it is.

blocks.h: Strict liability, and the word that must be used carefully

blocks.p: Strict liability means liability without proof of fault - it does not mean absolute liability, because Article 10 admits three defences. Note the contrast with the Bunkers Convention, where the liable "shipowner" is defined widely to include the registered owner, bareboat charterer, manager and operator jointly and severally, and only the insurance duty falls on the registered owner alone. Under Nairobi and under CLC the registered owner is the correct focus; under Bunkers it is not, and that distinction has been examined.

blocks.h: Two different ways the owner escapes - and they are not the same thing

blocks.p: Candidates blur Article 10 with Article 11. They do different work.

rows: What it does
The Convention applies, but the owner is not liable on these facts
The Convention stands down because another liability regime governs
Grounds

Act of war or hostilities; an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible natural phenomenon; damage wholly caused by a third party acting with intent; damage wholly caused by the negligence of an authority responsible for navigational aids
The costs are recoverable under CLC 1992, the HNS Convention, the Bunkers Convention, or the nuclear liability conventions
Effect on the coastal State
The State may still act, but recovers nothing from this owner under this Convention
The State recovers under the other regime instead, and is not left uncovered

blocks.p: The word to be careful with in Article 10 is wholly. Partial contribution by a third party does not release the owner; the defence requires the damage to have been caused entirely by that act or omission.

blocks.h: Wreck removal is not salvage, and the difference is examinable

rows: Nature of the act
Voluntary service to property in danger
Compulsory duty imposed on the registered owner
Who initiates
The salvor offers; the master or owner accepts
The affected State determines a hazard and sets a deadline
Payment
Reward, on the no-cure-no-pay principle, with special compensation for environmental effort
No reward - the owner bears the cost, strictly
Timing
While the property is still in danger and can be saved
After the casualty, once the wreck is a hazard

blocks.p: The two meet in Article 9, which preserves the owner's right to contract with a salvor or contractor of his own choice for the removal, subject to conditions imposed by the State. So the commercial salvage market still does the work - it is the obligation and the bill that the Convention allocates.

ul: Omitting the fourth category - a ship about to sink or strand - and so defining only what is already on the bottom.
Saying the Convention applies in territorial waters. It applies in the EEZ; the territorial sea is an opt-in under Article 3(2).
Treating every wreck as removable. Without a hazard there is no removal obligation.
Writing limb (c) as one paragraph about pollution, leaving the coastal State's responsibilities unstated.
Confusing the Nairobi regime with salvage. Salvage is a voluntary service for reward; wreck removal is a compulsory duty imposed on the owner.
Asking which conventions displace Nairobi - CLC 1992, HNS, Bunkers and the nuclear conventions, under Article 11.
Asking whether liability is unlimited. It is not: Article 10(2) expressly preserves limitation under the applicable regime.
Asking for the time limits and expecting only one. There are two - three years and six years, measured from different events.
Asking who reports the wreck. The master or operator of the ship, to the affected State - not the coastal State to the owner.

Your ship strands in another State's EEZ. What are your first duties as Chief Engineer and what does the company have to do?
Can the coastal State remove the wreck before the deadline expires?
How does the wreck removal insurance relate to P&I cover?
Which Indian statute governs wreck and salvage, and who is the Receiver of Wreck?

blocks.p: Casualty, then hazard, then four verbs. Nothing is a wreck without a maritime casualty; nothing must be removed unless it is a hazard; and once both are satisfied the Convention is just report, locate, mark, remove. Hang the money on the end: owner strictly liable, 300 GT insurance, direct action, three and six years.

questions.understand_first: A wreck is not primarily an environmental problem in this Convention - it is an unallocated bill. Before 2015 a ship could sink outside a coastal State's territorial sea, in water that State polices but does not own, and there was no clear international power to compel the owner to move it and no certainty that anybody solvent would pay. UNCLOS gave the coastal State rights in the exclusive economic zone but no removal machinery. The Nairobi Convention supplies the machinery, and the whole of it turns on one word: HAZARD. A wreck that endangers nothing is left alone. Once it is a hazard, four things follow mechanically - report it, locate it, mark it, remove it - and the registered owner pays, whether or not anyone was at fault, backed by insurance the State can sue directly. Read the question that way and limb (c) writes itself: the owner carries the cost and the liability, the coastal State carries the judgement and the power to act, and the environment is the reason both exist.

blocks.h: 1. The instrument and its state at this sitting

blocks.p: The Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims, 1976 was adopted on 19 November 1976 and entered into force on 1 December 1986. The Protocol of 1996, in force 13 May 2004, raised the limits substantially and introduced a tacit acceptance procedure for raising them again. Under that procedure the limits were raised by the 2012 amendments, which entered into force on 8 June 2015. Those are the limits applicable at the date of this examination. India is a party to the Convention as amended, and it is given domestic effect through the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.

blocks.h: 2. Objectives - why limitation exists at all

blocks.p: A single maritime occurrence can generate loss out of all proportion to the value of the ship - a berth destroyed, a fairway blocked, another vessel sunk, lives lost. An unbounded exposure is an uninsurable one, and an uninsured claim is worth nothing. The Convention therefore exists to:

ul: make catastrophic maritime exposure insurable, so that the money is actually there;
give claimants a certain fund in place of an uncertain full recovery against a possibly worthless defendant;
secure uniformity, so that the ceiling does not depend on which court is seised;
keep shipowners trading and salvors willing to intervene, by capping the downside of both;
strike a deliberate balance: limits materially higher than those of the 1957 regime, granted in exchange for a right to limit that is almost impossible to break.

blocks.p: That last point is the heart of the 1976 Convention. Under the earlier regime a claimant could break limitation by showing the owner's "actual fault or privity", which invited litigation in every serious casualty. LLMC 1976 replaced the test with a far harder one, and paid for the change with higher limits.

ul: Who may limit (Art 1). Shipowners - defined to include the owner, charterer, manager and operator - together with salvors, any person for whose act the owner or salvor is responsible, and the liability insurer, who may limit to the same extent as the assured.
The measure is tonnage. The limits are a function of the ship's gross tonnage, calculated under Annex I to the Tonnage Convention 1969 - not deadweight and not displacement.
Global, per occurrence. The cap applies to the aggregate of all claims arising on any distinct occasion (Art 9), not claim by claim.
Separate funds. Loss of life and personal injury has its own, higher, fund; all other claims share a lower one; passenger claims are dealt with separately again under Article 7.
The right is nearly unbreakable (Art 4). See section 6.
A fund need not be constituted (Art 10). Limitation may be invoked as a defence without depositing money, although national law may require constitution.

blocks.p: Article 2(1) makes the following limitable whatever the basis of liability - contract, tort or statute:

ul: claims for loss of life or personal injury, or loss of or damage to property - expressly including damage to harbour works, basins, waterways and aids to navigation - occurring on board or in direct connexion with the operation of the ship or with salvage operations, and consequential loss;
claims for loss resulting from delay in the carriage by sea of cargo, passengers or their luggage;
claims for loss resulting from infringement of rights other than contractual rights, occurring in direct connexion with the operation of the ship or salvage operations;
claims for the raising, removal, destruction or rendering harmless of a ship which is sunk, wrecked, stranded or abandoned, including anything that is or has been on board;
claims for the removal, destruction or rendering harmless of the cargo;
claims by a person other than the person liable for measures taken to avert or minimise loss for which that person could limit, and further loss caused by those measures.

blocks.p: Article 3 takes five categories outside the Convention altogether:

rows: Salvage - including special compensation under Article 14 of the Salvage Convention 1989 - and contribution in general average
Both exist to reward voluntary intervention that benefits everyone. Capping them would discourage the very act the law is trying to buy
Oil pollution damage within the meaning of the CLC
The CLC provides its own strict-liability regime, its own limitation fund and its own compulsory insurance, and the IOPC Fund sits above it. Two regimes over one claim would be incoherent
Nuclear damage claims governed by an international convention or by national law that governs or prohibits limitation
Nuclear liability is a separate treaty system with its own channelling rules
Claims against the owner of a nuclear ship for nuclear damage
Same reason

Claims by servants of the shipowner or salvor whose duties are connected with the ship or the salvage operations, and by their dependants, where the law governing the contract of service denies limitation or fixes a higher one
Employment claims are protected by the law of the service contract, which the Convention declines to cut down

blocks.p: One further qualification is easily missed. Article 18(1) permits a State Party to reserve the right to exclude the wreck-removal and cargo-removal heads at Article 2(1)(d) and (e). Where that reservation has been made those claims are not limitable in that State, which is why wreck removal liability can be capped in one jurisdiction and uncapped in another.

blocks.h: 6. Conduct barring limitation - the reason the list matters

blocks.p: Article 4 provides that a person liable is not entitled to limit if the loss resulted from his personal act or omission, committed either with intent to cause such loss, or recklessly and with knowledge that such loss would probably result. Three features make this near-unbreakable: the conduct must be that of the person seeking to limit and not of the master or crew; recklessness alone is not enough without knowledge of the probable consequence; and the burden of proving it lies on the claimant. Negligent navigation, poor maintenance or a badly run ship will not by themselves defeat limitation.

Constituting the fund (Art 11). A person alleged to be liable may constitute a fund with the court or other competent authority in any State Party where legal proceedings are instituted, either by depositing the sum or by producing a guarantee acceptable to that authority. The fund must equal the applicable limits for all claims arising from the occurrence, together with interest from the date of the occurrence to the date of constitution. A fund constituted by one person is deemed constituted by all persons entitled to limit for the same occurrence.

Consequences (Arts 12, 13, 14). The fund is distributed rateably among the established claims. Once it is constituted, a claimant may not pursue the person's other assets, and any ship or property arrested must be released. Constitution and distribution are governed by the law of the State Party in which the fund is constituted.

Calculating the amount (Arts 6 and 7, as amended by the 1996 Protocol). Two separate limits are computed on the ship's gross tonnage in successive bands, and the unit of account is the Special Drawing Right, converted as at the date the fund is constituted:

rows: Up to 2,000
3.02 million SDR
1.51 million SDR
plus 1,208 SDR per ton
plus 604 SDR per ton
plus 906 SDR per ton
plus 453 SDR per ton
Over 70,000
plus 604 SDR per ton
plus 302 SDR per ton

blocks.p: These are the figures produced by the 2012 amendments in force from 8 June 2015. Where the personal-claims fund is insufficient, the unpaid balance of those claims ranks rateably with the property claims against the property fund - so life and injury claims are preferred, but not to the exclusion of everything else. Passenger claims are calculated differently again under Article 7: a fixed sum of 175,000 SDR multiplied by the number of passengers the ship is certified to carry, the 1996 Protocol having removed the overall monetary cap that the 1976 text imposed.

The method, rather than the figures, is what the examiner is testing: identify the ship's gross tonnage, decide which fund the claim falls into, work upward through the bands, add interest from the occurrence, and remember that passengers are computed on certified capacity and not on tonnage at all.

Limb (b) carries 6 of the 16 marks and asks two questions in one sentence - which claims are subject to limitation, and which are excluded. Splitting it into two separately headed sections is the single highest-value structural decision in this answer, because an examiner marking a list can only credit what is visible as a list. Article 4 is then given its own short section: it belongs with the exceptions in logic - it is the other way limitation fails - but it is not part of the Article 3 enumeration and merging them muddles both.

Every part of LLMC follows from one trade: higher limits in exchange for a right that is almost impossible to break. If you can state that, you can derive the objectives, explain why Article 4 is worded so severely, and explain why the 1996 Protocol needed a tacit acceptance mechanism - a bargain built on fixed sums decays with inflation unless the sums can be raised without a new conference.

blocks.h: Three limitations that are not the same thing

rows: LLMC global limitation
The aggregate of all claims from one occurrence, against the shipowner and those entitled with him
Gross tonnage, in bands
Carrier package limitation (Hague-Visby and the Indian Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925)
The carrier's liability for cargo, per package or unit or per kilogramme
Packages, units or weight
CLC limitation
Oil pollution damage from a laden tanker - and the reason such claims are outside LLMC
Tonnage, under its own scale

blocks.p: They stack: a cargo claim may be reduced first by package limitation and then again by the global fund. Treating them as alternatives is a common error.

ul: Answering limb (b) with only the Article 2 list and never reaching Article 3.
Saying oil pollution is limitable under LLMC. Pollution damage within the meaning of the CLC is excluded - but a bunker spill from a ship outside CLC is not excluded by Article 3.
Saying the right is lost by negligence, or by the master's recklessness. Article 4 requires the personal act or omission of the person seeking to limit.
Quoting one tonnage figure and forgetting that there are two funds plus a separate passenger limit.
Confusing constitution of the fund (Art 11) with the right to limit (Art 10). The right exists without a fund; the fund is what bars other actions.
Calling the unit of account "dollars". It is the SDR, converted at the date the fund is constituted.
Asking whether the insurer may limit. Yes - Article 1(6), to the same extent as the assured.
Asking whether a salvor may limit when not operating from a ship. Yes - the 1976 Convention was drafted to cover salvors after The Tojo Maru, and salvage operations are expressly within Article 2.
Asking whether wreck removal is limitable. It is in the Article 2 list, but Article 18(1) lets a State reserve it out - so the honest answer names the reservation.
Asking what happens if the personal-injury fund runs out. The balance ranks rateably against the property fund; it is not simply lost.
Asking which convention pays the salvor in full. Salvage and general average are excluded by Article 3 precisely so that they are not cut down.
Your ship damages a lock gate and a berth. Which fund does the port authority claim against, and what determines its size?
A crew member is injured. Can the owner limit against that claim?
What is an SDR, and when is it converted?
Which Indian statute gives effect to the limitation regime?
How does the LLMC fund interact with the P&I club's cover?
Why is special compensation under Article 14 of the Salvage Convention outside LLMC?

blocks.p: Five questions in order: why, who, what is in, what is out, how much. For the exceptions, remember the logic rather than the list - somebody else pays (CLC, nuclear) or capping it would defeat the purpose (salvage, general average, the owner's own crew). For the fund, remember two funds plus passengers: tonnage bands for the first two, certified passenger capacity for the third.

questions.understand_first: Limitation of liability is the oldest bargain in shipping law and it is not a loophole. A single ship can destroy a berth, sink another vessel, kill people and block a fairway in one afternoon; the exposure is unbounded, and no insurer can price an unbounded risk. If liability were unlimited, either the cover would not exist or its cost would sit on every tonne of cargo carried. So the international community fixed a ceiling and made it predictable: a claimant gets less than full compensation, but gets it from a fund that certainly exists. The 1976 Convention sharpened the bargain deliberately - the older test let a claimant break limitation by proving ordinary "actual fault or privity", which produced litigation in every casualty. LLMC 1976 made the right almost unbreakable in exchange for higher limits, and the 1996 Protocol raised those limits again. Read every part of this question through that trade and the structure follows: what the ceiling covers (Art 2), what it deliberately does not cover because another regime pays or because the claim would destroy the bargain (Art 3), when the right is forfeited (Art 4), and how much money the ceiling actually is (Arts 6, 7 and 11).

blocks.h: 1. Two schemes that are not two versions of one thing

blocks.p: The names are one letter apart and the schemes are opposites. The Condition Assessment Scheme (CAS) is mandatory international law, created by IMO, compelled by MARPOL Annex I and administered by the flag Administration. The Condition Assessment Programme (CAP) is a voluntary commercial product sold by classification societies and bought by owners because the market asks for it. CAS answers the question may this ship continue to trade?; CAP answers how good is this ship? Neither replaces the statutory survey regime or the enhanced survey programme, and neither is a survey in the SOLAS sense - each is a scheme built around one.

Purpose. CAS was developed after the Erika and tightened after the Prestige, and adopted by resolution MEPC.94(46), as subsequently amended. Its purpose is to provide the Administration with an independent, prescribed and auditable verification that the structural condition of an ageing single-hull oil tanker is adequate - so that a ship which MARPOL would otherwise have retired may continue to carry oil only on measured evidence rather than on the strength of a clean class record.

Applicability. It is made compulsory by MARPOL Annex I regulation 20 for the single-hull categories permitted to continue trading beyond their phase-out date, and by regulation 21 in connection with the carriage of heavy grade oil. Ships come into scope on age and category, not by choice.

Scope. Deliberately narrow. CAS looks at the hull: extensive close-up survey, thickness measurement against prescribed acceptance criteria, the condition of coatings and corrosion-prevention arrangements, and the resulting structural strength. It is carried out in conjunction with the enhanced survey programme intermediate or renewal survey and is additional to it. The outcome is binary: the Administration reviews the Final Report and issues - or refuses - a Statement of Compliance.

Purpose. CAP exists because age alone is a poor proxy for condition, and the market needs a better one. Charterers, oil majors operating vetting regimes, banks financing tonnage and buyers in the second-hand market all want independent evidence that a fifteen-year-old ship is materially better than her age implies. CAP supplies it as a graded, documented assessment.

Scope. Far wider than CAS. A full CAP typically assesses hull structure, machinery and cargo systems, and often electrical and cargo-handling equipment, each rated separately. The assessment goes well beyond class minimum: thickness measurement at a density greater than survey requires, strength and fatigue evaluation of the structure, performance testing and functional trials of machinery, and examination of maintenance records. The outcome is a graded rating - commonly a four-point scale on which the best grade denotes condition very much better than the classification minimum. It carries no statutory effect whatever.

CAS is triggered by law and by the ship's objective characteristics: her single-hull category, her age relative to the regulation 20 phase-out, and whether she is engaged in the carriage of heavy grade oil under regulation 21. It cannot be declined, deferred by agreement, or narrowed to save cost. CAP is triggered by a commercial decision - a charterer's requirement, an oil major's vetting regime, a lender's condition, an intended sale, or simply an owner wishing to evidence quality. It need never be taken at all.

blocks.p: Ship safety. Both schemes replace an inference from age with a measurement of condition. Wastage, fatigue cracking, coating breakdown and locally deficient structure are found by close-up survey and gauging early enough to be repaired rather than discovered by failure. The prescribed, plan-driven scope of CAS in particular removes the discretion that lets a difficult tank go unexamined for another cycle.

Environmental protection. This is the reason CAS exists at all. The single-hull tanker casualties of 1999 and 2002 were structural failures of ageing ships, and the regulatory response was to make continued trading conditional on demonstrated structural fitness. CAP contributes the same effect through the market: a charterer that will not fix an unrated ship of a certain age imposes a condition standard without legislating one.

Operational efficiency. The measured data has commercial value beyond compliance. It supports vetting outcomes and charter access; it converts dry-dock and steel-renewal planning from guesswork into a budgeted programme; it provides credible residual-life and valuation evidence for sale, purchase and finance, and useful information for underwriters; and by finding defects on a planned basis it reduces unplanned repair and off-hire. Both schemes, in short, convert an opinion about an old ship into documented evidence.

ul: The CAS survey plan. Prepared by the owner in co-operation with the Administration or its recognized organization and submitted well in advance of the survey - the Scheme specifies a lead time of five months. It sets out the ship's particulars and service history, the structural condition and repair history, previous thickness measurement results, the tanks to be examined, the extent of close-up survey and the measurement locations, and the arrangements for access and safety.

Documentation assembled. The survey report file and the ESP file; previous survey and thickness measurement reports; the history of structural repairs and modifications; records of coating condition and of the corrosion-prevention arrangements in each tank; and details of the cargoes carried and the tanks' service.
Thickness measurement arrangements. The measurement firm approved, and the measurement locations agreed with the attending surveyor, before gauging begins.

Physical preparation of the spaces. Tanks cleaned and gas-freed, ventilated and their atmospheres monitored continuously; adequate lighting provided; and safe access for close-up survey arranged by staging, rafting or other approved means, with the permit-to-work and rescue arrangements in place.
Scheduling and attendance. The work is planned to fall within the ESP intermediate or renewal survey, with attendance arranged for the Administration or its recognized organization.
Completion. The Final Report is submitted to the Administration, which reviews it and, if satisfied, issues the Statement of Compliance that permits the ship to continue trading.

blocks.p: Four printed limbs need four visible regions, and the temptation on a question like this is to write one long essay about old tankers. The single most valuable structural decision is section 1: stating the law versus commerce contrast before either scheme is described. It costs three sentences and it makes every subsequent difference in limb (b) read as a consequence rather than as a list of unrelated facts. Limb (b) names three axes - triggers, survey requirements, reporting procedures - so the answer uses those three words rather than inventing its own comparison headings.

blocks.h: Where each scheme sits in the survey architecture

blocks.p: A useful mental stack, from the bottom up: classification survey keeps the ship in class; the enhanced survey programme (ESP Code, resolution A.1049(27), made mandatory through SOLAS XI-1/2) prescribes the close-up and gauging regime for tankers and bulk carriers; CAS sits on top of the ESP survey for a defined class of ageing single-hull tanker and adds a State-verified structural pass; and CAP sits outside the statutory stack altogether, buying a graded assessment for commercial purposes. Only the first three are compulsory, and only the middle two are surveys.

blocks.h: Why the outcomes differ - pass versus grade

blocks.p: The difference in outcome is not cosmetic. A regulator needs a binary answer, because a ship is either permitted to trade or not; a grading would leave the Administration deciding how much wastage is acceptable in each case, which is exactly the discretion the Scheme was written to remove. A charterer needs the opposite - a ranking, because it is choosing between ships that are all lawfully entitled to trade. Explaining that in one sentence usually earns more than another paragraph of description.

ul: Presenting CAP and CAS as two flavours of the same survey.
Saying CAS replaces the enhanced survey programme. It is carried out within it and is additional to it.
Giving CAP a statutory effect - a CAP rating is not a certificate and does not permit or prohibit anything.
Applying CAS to double-hull tankers or to bulk carriers. Its trigger is the single-hull category under regulation 20 and the heavy-grade-oil carriage under regulation 21.
Writing limb (c) as a paragraph on safety only. The stem names three benefit headings and expects all three.
Skipping limb (d) for time. It is the smallest limb but it is a plain list - the cheapest marks on the question.
Asking who issues the Statement of Compliance. The Administration, after reviewing the Final Report - not the classification society on its own authority.
Asking what happens if CAS is failed. The ship may not continue in the trade that required it; there is no graded outcome to fall back on.
Asking whether CAP is recognised by IMO. It is not - it is a class and market instrument.
Asking what CAS actually measures. Structure. Machinery condition is a CAP question, not a CAS one.
Asking when the survey plan must be submitted, expecting a lead time rather than "before the survey".

CAP has no single authoritative text. The four-grade rating convention and the roughly fifteen-year trigger are common industry practice and vary between classification societies; they are described here as practice and must not be quoted as a rule.

Nothing in this regime changed in the two years before the January 2025 sitting. Two later MIW answers - November 2025 and March 2026 - compare ESP with CAP, which is a different comparison from the one printed here; neither was used, and neither should be pulled back onto this paper.

questions.understand_first: The two acronyms differ by one letter and by everything else. CAS is law and CAP is commerce. CAS - the Condition Assessment Scheme - was written after the Erika and hardened after the Prestige, and it exists for one purpose: to let a State satisfy itself that an ageing single-hull oil tanker that MARPOL would otherwise have retired is still structurally fit to carry oil. It is compulsory, it is administered by the flag Administration rather than by class alone, it looks only at structure, and it produces a pass: a Statement of Compliance, or nothing. CAP - the Condition Assessment Programme - is a voluntary classification-society product that an owner buys because charterers, oil majors, banks and buyers want independent evidence that a fifteen-year-old ship is better than her age suggests. It covers structure and machinery and cargo systems, and it produces a grade, not a pass. Hold that contrast - compulsory / voluntary, State / class, structure / whole ship, pass / grade - and all four limbs fall out of it.

steps.title: Two schemes that are not two versions of one thing
points: CAS is mandatory, created by IMO under MARPOL Annex I, administered by the flag Administration
CAP is voluntary, created and sold by classification societies, driven by charterers, vetting, finance and sale-and-purchase
CAS answers "may this ship still trade?"; CAP answers "how good is this ship?"
Neither replaces the statutory survey regime or the enhanced survey programme

steps.title: CAS - purpose and scope
points: Adopted by resolution MEPC.94(46) as amended, following the Erika casualty
Made compulsory by MARPOL Annex I regulation 20 for the single-hull categories permitted to continue trading beyond their phase-out date, and by regulation 21 for the carriage of heavy grade oil
Scope is deliberately narrow - the structural condition of the hull: close-up survey, thickness measurement, coating and corrosion-prevention condition, structural strength
Run in conjunction with the ESP intermediate or renewal survey, and additional to it
Outcome is a binary Statement of Compliance issued by the Administration after it reviews the Final Report

steps.title: CAP - purpose and scope
points: A voluntary classification-society programme with no statutory force
Typically taken up on tankers and bulk carriers from about fifteen years of age, when charterers begin to discriminate on age
Scope is wide - hull structure, machinery, cargo systems, and often electrical and cargo-handling equipment, each assessed separately
Assessment is far deeper than class minimum: extensive thickness measurement, strength and fatigue evaluation, performance testing of machinery, functional trials
Outcome is a graded rating, commonly on a four-point scale where the best grade denotes condition very much better than the class minimum

steps.title: Difference one - what triggers each
points: CAS is triggered by law and by the ship's objective characteristics: single-hull category, age and phase-out date under regulation 20, or carriage of heavy grade oil under regulation 21
CAP is triggered by a commercial decision - a charterer's requirement, an oil major's vetting regime, a bank's condition of finance, a sale, or the owner's own wish to evidence quality
CAS cannot be declined; CAP need never be taken at all

steps.title: Differences two and three - survey requirements and reporting
points: CAS: survey plan agreed in advance with the Administration and submitted well before the survey; conducted within the ESP intermediate or renewal survey; prescribed close-up and thickness measurement scope
CAP: scope set by the society's own programme and by what the owner buys; may extend to machinery running trials that CAS never touches
CAS reporting: Final Report to the Administration, which reviews it and issues or refuses the Statement of Compliance; the Organization may be furnished with a copy and may review
CAP reporting: a detailed report and rating issued to the owner, disclosed commercially at the owner's discretion; no State involvement and no public register
Consequence of a poor outcome: CAS - the ship may not continue in that trade; CAP - the ship loses commercial standing but remains fully entitled to trade

steps.title: Benefits - safety, environment, operational efficiency
points: Safety: structural deterioration is found by measurement rather than inferred from age, and found early enough to repair
Environment: the schemes exist because ageing tankers broke up and spilled - CAS is the regulatory answer to that, CAP the commercial one

Operational efficiency: better vetting outcomes and charter access, evidence-based dry-dock and steel-renewal planning, credible residual-life and valuation data for sale and finance, and fewer unplanned repairs and off-hire
Both convert an opinion about an old ship into measured, documented evidence

steps.title: CAS - documentation and preparatory steps
points: The CAS survey plan, prepared by the owner with the Administration or its recognized organization and submitted in advance of the survey

Documentation assembled: survey report file and ESP file, previous survey and thickness measurement reports, structural repair and modification history, coating and corrosion-prevention condition records, and details of the tanks and their service
Approval of the thickness measurement firm and agreement of the measurement locations before work starts
Physical preparation: tank cleaning, gas-freeing, ventilation and continuous atmosphere monitoring, lighting, and safe access for close-up survey by staging, rafts or approved means
Attendance arranged for the Administration or its recognized organization, and the survey scheduled to fall within the ESP intermediate or renewal survey
On completion, the Final Report to the Administration for review and issue of the Statement of Compliance

blocks.h: 1. The Convention and its controls at this sitting

blocks.p: The International Convention on the Control of Harmful Anti-fouling Systems on Ships, 2001 entered into force on 17 September 2008. It prohibits or restricts the anti-fouling systems listed in Annex 1, and provides through Annex 4 for survey, certification and control of ships. Annex 1 originally targeted organotin compounds acting as biocides - the tributyltin systems whose effects on non-target shellfish caused the Convention to be written.

The 2021 amendments added cybutryne to Annex 1, entering into force on 1 January 2023. From that date a cybutryne-containing system may not be applied or re-applied. A ship already carrying one complies either by removing it or by applying an overcoating sealer that forms a barrier preventing the substance leaching, and must do so at the next scheduled renewal of the anti-fouling system, subject to a backstop of 60 months from last application. At the date of this examination the control is therefore in force but still inside its transition window - many ships lawfully continue to carry cybutryne systems applied before 2023.

blocks.h: 2. Why energy-efficiency regulation raised the stakes

blocks.p: Fouling is a propulsion problem first. Slime, weed and shell growth raise frictional resistance, so more power and more fuel are required to hold the same speed, and the effect grows steadily between dockings. Since MARPOL Annex VI regulation 23 (EEXI) and regulation 28 (CII) became operative, that extra fuel is no longer only a cost: the CII is computed from fuel consumed against distance and capacity, so a fouled hull worsens the annual rating directly, and a poor rating obliges the owner to produce a corrective action plan through the SEEMP. Hull and propeller condition has become a compliance variable.

The same surface is also the subject of the IMO biofouling guidelines - the 2011 Guidelines, revised at MEPC 80 in 2023 - which address the transfer of invasive aquatic species and remain recommendatory. So the owner is pushed to keep the hull clean by three separate forces, while the Convention narrows what may be used to do it.
Both are electrochemical methods of controlling corrosion, and both work by moving the metal's potential - in opposite directions.

rows: Principle
Shift the potential negative so the structure becomes the cathode of the cell and ceases to dissolve
Shift the potential positive into the passive region so a stable protective oxide film forms, and hold it there
Method
Sacrificial (galvanic) anodes of zinc, aluminium or magnesium; or impressed current with inert anodes, reference electrodes, a transformer-rectifier and a controller
A potentiostat holding the metal at a controlled potential against a reference electrode, with an inert cathode
Current
Supplies current; demand rises as coating breaks down
Needs a large current to passivate initially, then a very small current to maintain
Suitable metals
Most structural metals, including ordinary shipbuilding steel
Only metals that passivate - stainless steels, carbon steel in specific media
Suitable environment
Seawater and other conducting electrolytes
Media that permit passivity - typically strong acids and process chemicals. Chlorides break down passivity
Risk if wrongly set
Over-protection: alkali and hydrogen at the surface causing coating disbondment and, in high-strength steels, hydrogen embrittlement
Loss of control drives the metal into the active or transpassive region and corrosion accelerates rather than stopping
Use on ships
Standard - hull, sea chests, ballast tanks, rudders and coolers
Not used on hulls in seawater. Confined to chemical plant and certain tank service

blocks.p: The comparison is therefore asymmetric and should be stated as such: cathodic protection is the marine technique, and anodic protection is the one whose conditions a seawater hull cannot satisfy.

blocks.h: 4. Why the comparison matters to a paint scheme

blocks.p: The coating is the primary barrier and the cathodic system protects only what the coating fails to cover; the two are designed and commissioned as one system. The critical interaction runs the other way as well. An over-protecting cathodic system generates hydroxyl ions and hydrogen at the steel surface, and the resulting alkalinity lifts the coating from the substrate - cathodic disbondment - typically first in the halo around anodes and ICCP anode positions. A newly applied, fully compliant anti-fouling scheme can therefore be destroyed from underneath by a system intended to protect it. Anode and ICCP anode locations, dielectric shields, boot-topping treatment and the protective potential setting all belong in the coating specification.

blocks.h: 5. Applying a compliant scheme on an existing ship

blocks.p: On an existing ship the first question is not which paint to buy but what is already there.

ul: Establish the existing system. Read the Record of Anti-Fouling Systems, previous dry-dock specifications and paint receipts, and where necessary test the coating. Decide between complete removal and the sealer coat route permitted for a controlled system.

Dock and wash. High-pressure fresh-water washing to remove fouling, slime and the spent leached layer. Washings and removed coating containing controlled substances are hazardous waste: they are contained, collected and landed to a reception facility, not allowed into the dock basin.

Prepare the surface. Assess the condition of the existing anticorrosive; abrasive blast or sweep to the specified preparation grade where removal is required. Check surface profile, soluble salt contamination and dust to the specified standards before coating.

Control the environment. Steel temperature at least a few degrees above the dew point, with relative humidity and air and steel temperature inside the product data sheet window, throughout application and cure.

Apply the specified system in order. Anticorrosive primer, tie coat where the system requires one, then the anti-fouling coats - at the specified wet and dry film thickness and within the minimum and maximum overcoating intervals. Exceeding the maximum interval destroys intercoat adhesion just as surely as under-thickness destroys the leaching rate.

Treat the difficult areas. Stripe-coat edges, welds, cut-outs and rough areas; attend to sea chests and gratings, boot-topping and flat bottom; polish the propeller; renew sacrificial anodes and verify ICCP anodes and shields.
Respect the end of the process. Observe the minimum drying time before undocking and the immersion window specified for the anti-fouling coat.

blocks.h: 6. The additional supervision that makes it effective

blocks.p: A compliant product badly applied is neither compliant in practice nor effective, so the supervision is part of the specification:

ul: Verify the product before it is landed. Obtain the manufacturer's written declaration that the system contains no organotin compound acting as a biocide and no cybutryne, together with product and safety data sheets.
Appoint a qualified coating inspector and agree written hold points - after washing, after blasting, before each coat, and at completion - at which work stops until the stage is accepted.
Evidence the preparation by recorded surface profile, soluble salt and dust testing.

Evidence each coat by wet film thickness during application and dry film thickness after cure, measured to the specified acceptance rule, with holiday detection and adhesion testing where the specification calls for them.
Reconcile what was actually applied - batch numbers and quantities against delivery notes and the theoretical consumption - so that the certificate rests on evidence rather than on assumption.
Record it. Dated photographs and written inspection reports for each stage, retained on board.

Close the loop. Arrange the AFS survey so that the certificate and the Record are re-issued or endorsed, and confirm compatibility between the new coating and the cathodic protection arrangement before the system is put back into service.

blocks.h: 7. Documents and records that demonstrate compliance

rows: International Anti-fouling System Certificate
Ships of 400 GT and above engaged in international voyages
Issued by the Administration or its recognized organization after survey - the formal statement that the ship's system complies
Record of Anti-Fouling Systems
Attached to that certificate
The system actually applied, the date of application, the applicator and the place - the traceable history
Declaration on Anti-fouling System
Ships of 24 m or more in length but below 400 GT on international voyages
Signed by the owner or authorised agent, with supporting documentation such as the paint receipt or contractor's invoice

blocks.p: Behind those three sit the supporting records a surveyor or port State control officer will actually ask for: the manufacturer's product and safety data sheets and declaration of compliance; invoices, delivery notes and batch records; the dry-dock specification and the coating inspection reports; and, where the sealer route was taken, the record of the sealer and of the system beneath it. Related records that bear on the same surface include the Inventory of Hazardous Materials, which lists anti-fouling systems, and the SEEMP with its hull-cleaning and propeller-polishing records. The certificate and Record are re-issued or endorsed whenever the anti-fouling system is changed or replaced.

The stem contains an instruction that is easy to miss: "have received special focus with the recent developments of energy-efficiency regulations ... against this background discuss". That is the examiner asking for the connection to be made, and section 2 exists solely to make it. Limb (b) then carries 6 marks for two demands - the application process and the additional supervision - so it is answered in two separately headed sections. Splitting them is what stops the supervision content from being buried inside the process narrative, which is where it usually disappears.

blocks.h: The trap inside limb (a), and the honest way through it

blocks.p: A comparison question invites a symmetrical answer, and here symmetry would be false. Anodic protection is not used on ships' hulls, because it depends on maintaining passivity and chlorides destroy passivity. The high-scoring answer gives the electrochemistry of both fairly, then says plainly which one is the marine technique and why - and then, instead of stopping, connects it to the paint through cathodic disbondment. That connection is what turns an apparently irrelevant limb into part of the same question.

blocks.h: Compliance is a property of the system, not of the tin

blocks.p: The phrase "AFS Convention-compliant paint" is slightly misleading. The Convention controls the anti-fouling system - what is on the hull, including what lies underneath. That is why an existing ship has two lawful routes: remove the controlled system, or seal it under a barrier coat. An owner who buys a compliant top coat and sprays it over a cybutryne system without a proper sealer has not achieved compliance, and the Record of Anti-Fouling Systems is where that shows.

blocks.p: Run the hull from the outside in and then from the dock to the filing cabinet. What is banned (organotin, then cybutryne) - why it matters now (CII) - how the steel is protected (cathodic, not anodic) - how the paint goes on (wash, prepare, control, apply, detail, dry) - who watches (declaration, inspector, hold points, thickness, batches) - what is filed (certificate, record, declaration). Three documents and two thresholds: 400 GT and 24 m.

questions.understand_first: Two things sit in this question that look separate and are not. Fouling is a fuel problem before it is an environmental one: a fouled hull can add tens of per cent to propulsive power for the same speed, and since MARPOL Annex VI made EEXI and CII operative that extra fuel is no longer just a cost - it moves the ship's annual rating and can force a corrective action plan. So the pressure to keep hulls clean has risen at exactly the moment the AFS Convention has narrowed what may be used to do it: organotins first, and now cybutryne. That squeeze - rising pressure to keep the hull clean, falling permission to use the chemistry that did it - is the background the question is built on. Cathodic and anodic protection are corrosion techniques, not anti-fouling ones, and only one of them is used on a ship's hull at all - but both share the same steel surface as the paint, are set up in the same dry dock, and a cathodic system that is over-protecting will destroy the coating it sits under. The comparison is therefore not a digression: it is the reason a compliant paint scheme still fails if the rest of the hull system is wrong.

steps.title: The Convention and its controls at this sitting
points: AFS Convention 2001, in force 17 September 2008 - controls harmful anti-fouling systems and provides for survey, certification and control
Annex 1 originally prohibited organotin compounds acting as biocides
The 2021 amendments added CYBUTRYNE to Annex 1, in force 1 January 2023
From that date it may not be applied or re-applied; ships already carrying it comply by removal or by an overcoating sealer at the next scheduled renewal of the system, subject to a 60-month backstop
So at this sitting the control is in force but its transition is still running

steps.title: Why energy-efficiency regulation raised the stakes
points: Fouling increases frictional resistance and therefore power and fuel for a given speed
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 23 (EEXI) and regulation 28 (CII) are in force and the CII rating runs annually
A fouled hull worsens the CII rating directly, and a D or E outcome drives a corrective action plan through the SEEMP
Hull and propeller condition is therefore a compliance variable and not only a fuel bill
The biofouling guidelines - 2011, revised 2023 - address the same surface from the invasive-species side and remain recommendatory

steps.title: Cathodic and anodic protection compared
points: Both are electrochemical, and both work by moving the metal's potential - but in opposite directions
CATHODIC protection drives the potential NEGATIVE so the structure becomes the cathode and stops dissolving
Two forms - sacrificial anodes of zinc, aluminium or magnesium, and impressed current with inert anodes, reference electrodes and a controller
ANODIC protection drives the potential POSITIVE into the passive region so a protective oxide film forms and is maintained
Anodic protection needs a metal that passivates and an electrolyte that permits it; chlorides break passivity, so it is used in chemical plant and some cargo tank service, NOT on hulls in seawater

steps.title: Why the comparison matters to a paint scheme
points: The coating is the primary barrier; cathodic protection covers only what the coating fails to cover
Over-protection generates alkali and hydrogen at the steel surface and causes cathodic disbondment - the coating lifts
So the cathodic system must be set and monitored to the correct protective potential, not simply turned up
Anode and ICCP anode locations, shields and boot-topping treatment are part of the coating specification, not separate from it
A compliant anti-fouling scheme over a badly protected hull still fails; the two systems are commissioned together

steps.title: Applying a compliant scheme on an existing ship
points: Establish what is already on the hull - the Record of Anti-Fouling Systems, previous specifications and paint receipts - and decide between REMOVAL and a SEALER COAT
Dry dock, high-pressure fresh-water wash to remove fouling, slime and the leached layer, with the washings and spent coating contained and landed as hazardous waste
Assess coating condition; abrasive blast or sweep to the specified preparation grade where removal is required, with surface profile and cleanliness checked
Control the environment - steel temperature above the dew point, humidity and temperature within the product data sheet limits

Apply the specified system in order: anticorrosive primer, tie coat where required, then the anti-fouling coats, at the specified wet and dry film thickness and within the minimum and maximum overcoating intervals
Stripe-coat edges, welds and cut-outs; treat sea chests, gratings, the boot-topping and the flat bottom; polish the propeller; renew or verify anodes and ICCP shields
Observe the minimum drying time before undocking and the immersion window in the data sheet

steps.title: The additional supervision that makes it effective
points: Obtain the manufacturer's written declaration that the product contains no organotin biocide and no cybutryne, with product and safety data sheets, before any paint is landed
Appoint a qualified coating inspector and agree written hold points - after wash, after blast, before each coat, and at completion
Verify preparation by profile, soluble salt and dust testing, and record the results
Verify each coat by wet film thickness during application and dry film thickness after, to the specified acceptance rule, with holiday detection and adhesion checks where specified
Verify batch numbers and quantities against the delivery notes so that what was specified is what was actually applied
Keep a dated photographic and written record, and have the AFS survey carried out so the certificate and Record are re-issued or endorsed
Confirm compatibility between the anti-fouling system and the cathodic protection arrangement before commissioning

steps.title: Documents and records that demonstrate compliance
points: International Anti-fouling System Certificate - ships of 400 GT and above on international voyages, issued by the Administration or its recognized organization after survey
Record of Anti-Fouling Systems - attached to the certificate; identifies the system applied, the date, the applicator and the place of application
Declaration on Anti-fouling System - ships of 24 m or more in length but below 400 GT on international voyages, signed by the owner or authorised agent and supported by documentation
Supporting evidence: manufacturer's product and safety data sheets, the declaration of compliance, invoices and delivery notes, and the dry-dock and coating inspection reports
Where a sealer coat was used, the record of the sealer and of the system beneath it
Related records the inspector will look at: the Inventory of Hazardous Materials, and the SEEMP with hull-cleaning and propeller-polishing records
Certificates and records are re-issued or endorsed when the anti-fouling system is changed or replaced

blocks.h: 1. What FSA is, and what it is not

blocks.p: Formal Safety Assessment is a structured and systematic methodology for enhancing maritime safety - including protection of life, health, the marine environment and property - by the use of risk analysis and cost-benefit assessment. It is set out in the Revised Guidelines for Formal Safety Assessment for use in the IMO rule-making process, MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2 of 2018.

Three characteristics define it. It is proactive - applied before a casualty rather than after one. It is applied to a generic ship type or system, not to a single vessel. And its purpose is to give the Organization a rational, transparent and traceable basis for deciding whether a proposed requirement is justified. Equally important is what it is not: FSA is not the risk assessment the ISM Code requires of a company, it is not mandatory on any ship, and its output is a recommendation to a Committee rather than a rule.

blocks.h: 2. The generic model - problem definition and five steps

blocks.p: The model begins with a preparatory step that is not numbered but decides everything after it: definition of the problem. This fixes the scope and boundaries, the generic ship model and its systems and functions, the operations and hazard categories in scope, and - critically - the risk acceptance criteria to be applied. Criteria are set before results are seen, so that the answer cannot be chosen after the fact.

rows: Hazard identification
A ranked list of hazards. Structured expert workshops using what-if and HAZOP-style techniques, screened by a risk index combining frequency and severity so that effort goes to what matters
Risk analysis
Quantified frequency and consequence for the ranked hazards; a risk contribution tree built from fault and event trees; identification of the high-risk areas and the influences that drive them
Risk control options
Risk control measures identified and grouped into coherent options, classified as preventive or mitigating, engineering or procedural, active or passive
Cost-benefit assessment
Each option costed over the life of the ship and set against the risk it removes, expressed through the cost-effectiveness indices
Recommendations for decision-making
A traceable case put to the Committee, including the assumptions, the sensitivity of the result and the uncertainty in the data

blocks.h: 3. Risk criteria and ALARP - the yardstick

blocks.p: Risk is frequency multiplied by consequence, and FSA expresses it in two ways: individual risk, the risk to a particular person, and societal risk, the risk of multi-fatality events, displayed on an F-N curve giving the frequency of accidents causing N or more fatalities. Against these are set three regions: intolerable, where the activity is not permitted at that level; tolerable if As Low As Reasonably Practicable; and negligible. In the ALARP region a control is adopted unless its cost is grossly disproportionate to the benefit - which is precisely the judgement that step 4 makes measurable.
These convert a risk control option into a single comparable number - money per unit of risk removed - so that competing options and competing proposals can be ranked on the same scale.

ul: GCAF - Gross Cost of Averting a Fatality. The cost of implementing and operating the option over the ship's life, divided by the reduction in expected fatalities it achieves.

NCAF - Net Cost of Averting a Fatality. The same calculation after subtracting the economic benefit the option itself produces - avoided damage, avoided cargo loss, avoided off-hire. An option that pays for part of itself has a lower NCAF than GCAF.

The criterion. An option is treated as cost-effective if the index falls below an agreed threshold, of the order of US$3 million per averted fatality, derived from societal indicators of what is spent to save a life and updated for inflation.
An environmental analogue - the cost of averting a tonne of oil spilled - has been proposed for pollution-driven assessments but has not been adopted by IMO as a criterion.

blocks.p: HRA is the systematic study of the human contribution to risk: what people are required to do, how they can fail to do it, why, and what would make failure less likely. It is not a sixth step - it runs through the model, contributing human-related hazards in step 1, human error probabilities in step 2, and human-centred risk control options in step 3.

It has a qualitative half - define the context, analyse the task, identify the possible errors and their causes - and a quantitative half, in which human error probabilities are assigned and then modified for performance shaping factors: fatigue and hours of rest, training and experience, the quality of procedures, ergonomic design of the interface, workload and time pressure, communication, and organisational culture. Its purpose is error reduction, not attribution of blame; the output is design, procedural and training measures.

Conventional task analysis decomposes a job into tasks and sub-tasks and records what the operator must do, in what order, with what information. Extended Task Analysis adds the context of each step: the equipment and its interface, the procedures and their usability, the information actually available at that moment, the physical environment, the training assumed, and the organisational pressures acting on the operator.

That context is where the performance shaping factors live, so XTA is the input that turns human error identification from a generic list into a specific one - it shows where errors are likely and why before anything is quantified. It is diagnostic rather than numerical, and it feeds the quantification methods that follow.

blocks.h: 7. Technique for Human Error Rate Prediction

blocks.p: THERP is the classical first-generation method for putting a number on the reliability of an operator task. Its procedure is:

ol: Break the task into sub-tasks, using the task analysis, and draw it as an HRA event tree in which each sub-task branches into success and failure.
Assign each failure branch a nominal human error probability from generic data tables for that class of action.
Modify the nominal values for the performance shaping factors applying to the real situation.
Apply the dependence model between successive actions - zero, low, moderate, high or complete - because an operator who has just made one error is more likely to make the next.
Credit genuine recovery factors: an alarm, an independent check, a second person.
Combine the branch probabilities to give the probability of task failure, which feeds the step 2 risk model.

blocks.p: Its strength is that it is transparent and auditable; its weakness is that it depends on generic data and on the analyst's judgement of the shaping factors and dependence.
These are the two complementary logic techniques on which step 2 is built, and they run in opposite directions.

blocks.p: Joined at the initiating event they form the bow-tie: causes on the left, consequences on the right. In FSA they build the risk contribution tree, which shows not only the total risk but which branch dominates it - and therefore where a risk control option should be aimed.

FMEA is inductive and bottom-up. Each component or function is taken in turn and examined for the ways it can fail. For every failure mode the analysis records the cause, the local effect, the effect on the system, the means of detection, the existing safeguards and the action required. FMECA extends it by adding criticality - severity, likelihood of occurrence and difficulty of detection combined into a risk priority number - so that limited effort can be ranked.

Its limitation is structural and examinable: FMEA looks at single failure modes, so combinations of failures and common-cause failures are outside it and must be caught by fault tree analysis. IMO requires FMEA in specific places - notably for high-speed craft - and it commonly supports the alternative design and arrangements approval route, where a design departing from the prescriptive rule must be shown to be at least as safe.

questions.understand_first: FSA is not a shipboard procedure and it is not the risk assessment the ISM Code asks a company for. It is the method IMO uses on itself - a structured way of deciding whether a proposed regulation is worth making, before it is made. That distinction is the first mark on the question and it also explains the shape of the method: a rule-maker cannot justify a requirement by saying it feels safer, so the method forces every step to produce something a committee can be shown. Find the hazards, size them, propose controls, price the controls against the risk they remove, and recommend. The six named terms are not a separate topic bolted on - they are the tools the middle steps run on, and they sit at different levels: cost effective indices live in step 4; fault trees, event trees and FMEA live in step 2; and HRA, with XTA feeding it and THERP quantifying it, runs through the whole model because the human being is present in every step. steps.title: What FSA is, and what it is not
points: A structured, systematic methodology for enhancing maritime safety - life, health, the marine environment and property - using risk analysis and cost-benefit assessment
Set out in the Revised Guidelines for FSA for use in the IMO rule-making process, MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2 of 2018
It is a tool for the ORGANIZATION's own rule-making: proactive, applied to a generic ship type rather than to one ship, and used to justify or reject a proposed requirement
It is NOT the ISM Code risk assessment a company performs on its own operations, and it is not mandatory on any ship

steps.title: The generic model - problem definition and five steps
points: Preparatory: define the problem - scope, boundaries, the generic ship model, the functions and systems in scope, and the risk acceptance criteria to be used
Step 1 - Hazard identification: structured expert workshops, what-if and HAZOP techniques, producing a ranked list of hazards by frequency and severity
Step 2 - Risk analysis: quantify the frequency and consequences of the ranked hazards, build the risk contribution tree, and find where the risk actually is
Step 3 - Risk control options: identify risk control measures and group them into coherent options - preventive or mitigating, engineering or procedural
Step 4 - Cost-benefit assessment: cost each option over the ship's life and set it against the risk it removes
Step 5 - Recommendations for decision-making: present the traceable case, with sensitivity and uncertainty, to the Committee
The output is a recommendation to a decision-maker, not a rule

steps.title: Risk criteria and ALARP - the yardstick
points: Risk is frequency multiplied by consequence, expressed as individual risk and as societal risk
Societal risk is displayed on F-N curves, the frequency of accidents causing N or more fatalities
Three regions - intolerable, tolerable if As Low As Reasonably Practicable, and negligible
In the ALARP region a control is adopted unless its cost is grossly disproportionate to the benefit, which is what step 4 measures
Without criteria the model produces numbers that mean nothing, which is why they are fixed in the preparatory step and not after the results are seen

steps.title: Cost effective indices
points: They convert a risk control option into a single comparable number: money per unit of risk removed
GCAF - Gross Cost of Averting a Fatality: the cost of the option divided by the reduction in expected fatalities over the ship's life
NCAF - Net Cost of Averting a Fatality: the same, after subtracting the economic benefit the option itself produces, such as avoided damage or lost hire
An option is judged cost-effective if the index falls below the criterion, which is of the order of US$3 million per averted fatality and is updated for inflation
An environmental analogue - the cost of averting a tonne of oil spilled - has been proposed but is not an adopted IMO criterion

steps.title: Human Reliability Analysis
points: The systematic study of the human contribution to risk: what people are required to do, how they fail, why, and what would reduce it
It runs across the whole model - human-related hazards in step 1, human error probabilities in step 2, and human-centred risk control options in step 3
Qualitative half: define the context, analyse the task, identify the possible errors and their causes
Quantitative half: assign human error probabilities and modify them for performance shaping factors - fatigue, training, procedures, ergonomics, workload, time pressure, organisational culture
Its purpose is error REDUCTION, not blame: the output is design, procedure and training measures

steps.title: Extended Task Analysis
points: Ordinary task analysis decomposes what the operator has to do into steps and sub-steps
Extended Task Analysis adds the CONTEXT of each step - the equipment and its interface, the procedures, the information available, the environment, the training and the organisation
That context is where performance shaping factors are found, so XTA is the input that makes human error identification specific rather than generic
It is qualitative and diagnostic: it tells you where errors are likely and why, before anything is quantified

steps.title: Technique for Human Error Rate Prediction
points: A first-generation human reliability quantification method - the classical way of putting a number on an operator task
The task is drawn as an HRA event tree of binary success and failure branches, one per sub-task
Each branch is given a nominal human error probability from generic data tables
The nominal values are modified for performance shaping factors and for the DEPENDENCE between successive actions, from zero through low, moderate and high to complete
Recovery factors - checks, alarms, a second person - are credited where they genuinely exist
Combining the branches gives the probability of task failure, which feeds the step 2 risk model

steps.title: Fault and event tree analysis
points: FAULT TREE - deductive and backward: start from one undesired top event and develop downward through AND and OR gates to the basic events that can cause it
It yields minimal cut sets - the smallest combinations of failures sufficient to cause the top event - and, with data, the top event probability
EVENT TREE - inductive and forward: start from an initiating event and branch through the success or failure of each safety barrier to a set of distinct outcomes with frequencies
Together they form the bow-tie: causes on the left, the initiating event at the centre, consequences on the right
In FSA they build the risk contribution tree in step 2 and show which branch dominates the risk

steps.title: Failure Mode and Effect Analysis
points: Inductive and bottom-up: take each component or function in turn and ask how it can fail
For each failure mode record the cause, the local effect, the effect on the system, the means of detection and the existing safeguards, then the action required
FMECA adds criticality - severity, occurrence and detectability combined into a risk priority number - so that effort can be ranked
Its limitation is structural: it examines SINGLE failures, so combinations and common-cause failures must be caught by fault tree analysis instead
IMO requires it in specific places, notably for high-speed craft, and it supports the alternative design and arrangements route
